theFourCp1IntentionsThatChangedWhenMeasu.cp1Said: the runner helper is withHeavyScanLease(client, spec, fn, {onEvent}) -- a callback wrapper.
theFourCp1IntentionsThatChangedWhenMeasu.shipped: grantHeavyScanLease(client, spec) returning a handle {holderToken, attachRun(runId), assertHeld(), close(outcome), state}.
theFourCp1IntentionsThatChangedWhenMeasu.whyItHadToChange: the jobs must take the lease BEFORE startRun and then hang the lease on the run row they get back. A callback wrapper owns the run id's scope and cannot receive it, so the announce event could not name the run it belongs to. The handle keeps the same finally discipline (close() releases and stops the timer) while letting the caller sequence take -> startRun -> attachRun -> work -> close.
theFourCp1IntentionsThatChangedWhenMeasu.consequenceForTheContract: AGENT-CONTRACT section 4's announce/confirm pair is still discharged, on run_events, but it is written by attachRun/the caller's own event hook rather than inside a wrapper.

theFourCp1IntentionsThatChangedWhenMeasu.shipped: canonicalStoreKey() plus storeRefFromUrl / storeRefFromEnv, and normalizeSpec now runs store through canonicalStoreKey.
theFourCp1IntentionsThatChangedWhenMeasu.whyItHadToChange: CP1 already keyed on the host, but the SESSION route makes the hole reachable: a job arrives with a connection URL and a session arrives with whatever a human typed (`host:port`). Deriving the key only on the URL path meant a session's `db.example.com:5432` and a job's `db.example.com` were TWO keys -- both would take successfully and both would scan, while every test still passed. The canonicalization is now the single derivation, and the raw spelling is kept as store_alias so a seat can recognise its own lease.
theFourCp1IntentionsThatChangedWhenMeasu.pinnedBy: test/heavy-lease.test.mjs 'EVERY door a caller can come through lands on one key' (six spellings incl. userinfo, case, path, IPv6) and test/p281-heavy-lease-api.test.mjs, where a job's URL takes the store and a session's host:port is refused and told by whom.

theFourCp1IntentionsThatChangedWhenMeasu.cp1Said: take = SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, then insert.
theFourCp1IntentionsThatChangedWhenMeasu.shipped: one transaction: UPDATE the expired unreleased rows for this store (release_kind='expired', released_by=taker, reap_reason recorded), then INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, and on zero rows re-read the blocking row and raise LEASE_HELD naming it, writing the refusal row in the same transaction.
theFourCp1IntentionsThatChangedWhenMeasu.whyItHadToChange: the partial unique index is the decision and the application must not be able to overrule it; ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING makes the index the arbiter in the same statement as the write, and the sweep of expired rows has to be inside that transaction or the taker's own insert would collide with the corpse it just decided to close.
theFourCp1IntentionsThatChangedWhenMeasu.evidence: F1 (two real processes, exactly one TAKEN), F2 (a taskkill /F'd holder: refused before expiry, taken after, corpse closed as expired).

theFourCp1IntentionsThatChangedWhenMeasu.cp1Said: constraints: (released_at IS NULL AND release_kind IS NULL) OR (released_at IS NOT NULL AND release_kind IN (...)).
theFourCp1IntentionsThatChangedWhenMeasu.shipped: the same, plus an EXPLICIT `release_kind IS NOT NULL` in the released arm.
theFourCp1IntentionsThatChangedWhenMeasu.whyItHadToChange: measured by a failing live test, not by reading: `release_kind IN ('released','expired','reaped')` evaluates to NULL when release_kind IS NULL, and a CHECK constraint PASSES on NULL. A row with released_at set and release_kind unset was therefore admissible -- a closed lease that does not say how it closed, which is the one thing this table exists to answer.
theFourCp1IntentionsThatChangedWhenMeasu.pinnedBy: test/p281-heavy-lease-live.test.mjs 'the CHECK constraints refuse the states the writer must never produce' (SQLSTATE 23514).

twoDefectsOnlyTheWholePathFound.defect: the session script's renew and release sent no x-factory-operator header, so the API answered 401 OPERATOR_REQUIRED. A seat could TAKE a heavy-scan window and then never refresh it or hand it back: the store would sit held until the TTL expired, so the control's only exit was a timeout.
twoDefectsOnlyTheWholePathFound.howItWasFound: the cross-repo run (real server + real store + the doc_repo script as a subprocess), not by any unit test -- the unit tests exercise the module and the API tests used the header directly.
twoDefectsOnlyTheWholePathFound.fixedBy: MUTATIONS in the session script carries an operator on every mutation (take/renew/release), and renew/release now REQUIRE --holder; the API's OPERATOR_REQUIRED is also mapped to 401 on the heavy routes (it was falling into the 500 arm), matching the POST verb route's existing behaviour.

twoDefectsOnlyTheWholePathFound.defect: the two heavy GET routes had no error handling, so a throw inside the async handler left the request unanswered AND became an unhandled rejection, which takes the control server down on modern Node. The server every route in the fleet depends on.
twoDefectsOnlyTheWholePathFound.howItWasFound: writing the live API test and asking what happens when the read cannot be served.
twoDefectsOnlyTheWholePathFound.fixedBy: both reads are wrapped and answer a coded 500; a read of an unknown holder_token is a 404 with a body, because 'I hold nothing' and 'my lease is gone' are different answers a caller must be able to tell apart.

LESSON: A CHECK constraint does not fire on NULL. `release_kind IN ('released','expired','reaped')` is NULL when release_kind is NULL, and a CHECK PASSES on NULL, so a released row with no release_kind was admissible until the constraint said `release_kind IS NOT NULL` explicitly. Any CHECK that guards 'a closed row must say how it closed' needs the NOT NULL spelled out (hauska-factory migrations/0013, 2026-09-16).

A guard keyed on a caller-supplied string is only as good as the derivation that produces it. Two spellings of one Postgres host are two keys, and two keys means two leases on one store means the guard silently does nothing while every test passes. Derive the key from the connection the caller is already using, and pin the spellings in a test (canonicalStoreKey, 2026-09-16).

An unwrapped `await` inside a node http handler is two failures at once: the request never gets an answer and the rejection takes the process down. Any new route in factory-control needs its own try/catch (src/control/api.mjs, 2026-09-16).

A helper that BOTH takes a lease and starts the run can take the lease too late: take it first, then startRun, then attach -- otherwise a refused scan leaves a run row claiming work that never happened (AGENT-CONTRACT section 4's 'announced before', 2026-09-16).
Testing a client against a server in the SAME process with spawnSync deadlocks: the child waits on a server whose event loop is blocked by the parent. Use async spawn (P:/tmp harness, 2026-09-16).
DEAD-END: Extending the existing `leases` table for heavy scans: its PRIMARY KEY (entity_type, county_fips) plus the leases_no_global CHECK cannot express 'per database, county optional' without weakening the guard on the writer scope, and its ON CONFLICT ... WHERE expires <= now() STEALS an expired lease silently, which is right for a writer and wrong for a rare exclusive window whose crash must be RECORDED. Read at CP1; re-litigating it costs a session.

Keying the lease on a declared alias ('cortex', 'factory'): cloudbuild.publish.yaml states at source that two env-vars point at one Neon project/branch, so an alias key lets one store carry two live heavy scans.
Vercel-style ping/keepalive for the session script: rejected in the session design; the window is held by a real row with an expiry, not by the script staying alive.
